podcast.title: George Bellamy (Matt's Father) – Played on "Telstar" (1962), Second British Song to Hit #1 in America
podcast.body: In 1961, Matt Bellamy's father George Bellamy, then a 20-year-old country singer, answered an ad in *Melody Maker* placed by legendary UK producer Joe Meek, who was assembling a studio group called the Tornados. George played rhythm guitar on "Telstar," an instrumental single released summer 1962, capitalizing on the excitement around the launch of the Telstar communications satellite. It became just the second British song to reach number one on the American charts and the second instrumental to top charts on both sides of the Atlantic, selling over 5 million copies worldwide. Joe Meek subsequently "went extra crazy" and the Tornados disintegrated; George ended up working as a plumber. "Tell Star was a massive hit, becoming just the second British song to reach number one on the American charts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation – Won Battle of the Bands as Rocket Baby Dolls (1994, Teignmouth)
podcast.body: In 1994, at the Broadmeadow Sports Centre in Teignmouth, Devon (population ~15,000), 16-year-olds Matt Bellamy, Christopher Wolstenholme, and Dominic Howard competed in a battle of the bands as "Rocket Baby Dolls" (evolved from "Fixed Penalty," itself evolved from "Gothic Plague"). They entered halfheartedly, thinking the concept idiotic, but the violence of their performance drew such a strong crowd response that they won — surprising themselves enough to take music seriously. About a week later they renamed themselves Muse. "They played with such violence and because the crowd responded so well to this violence, they ended up winning."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Demo Tape (May 1995) – Cassette Worth ~$1,000 Today
podcast.body: In May 1995, the band recorded four songs possibly under the guidance of Matt's father George ("Copyright Geo Bell Music" appears on the cassette label). The tape, titled *This Is a Muse Demo*, was distributed to promoters and venues across the northwest of England by their first manager Phil Corthals, securing more gigs and their first overseas show (in France). Very few copies were made; the cassette now sells for close to $1,000. "If you can find one, the asking price is close to $1,000."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cryptic Fan Codes and Hidden Messages – Bicycles Hidden Across America (2005 Tour)
podcast.body: On a 2005 tour, Muse printed coded set lists each night using fake song titles that were actually anagrams and cipher clues. Solving these led to email addresses, then to four autographed bicycles — the band's tour fitness bikes — hidden under abandoned railway bridges across America, with combination locks whose codes were embedded in the puzzles. One clue required fans to write "Christ" on their body, photograph it, and email the image to unlock the next clue; only four people worldwide solved that one. A harder puzzle directed the solver to a specific recording studio in England to claim a signed Muse guitar. For the launch of "United States of Eurasia," USB sticks were hidden in Berlin, Tokyo, Hong Kong, Moscow, Paris, and Dubai, each containing a code to enter on a website; once all codes were entered, parts of the new song were revealed. "Only four people worldwide succeeded in breaking that one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: World Record Guitar Destruction – 140 Guitars Smashed on 2010 Resistance Tour
podcast.body: Matt Bellamy holds the world record for the greatest number of guitars smashed on a single tour, destroying 140 during the 2010 leg of The Resistance Tour. "Matt Bellamy holds a world record for the greatest number of guitars smashed on a single tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ability to Fill Stadiums with Guitar Solos
podcast.body: Mios is noted as one of the few bands today capable of filling an 80,000-person stadium and having the audience enjoy an 8-minute guitar solo, which is considered a rare feat in contemporary music. "Son una, casi la única banda bien día, que son capaces de llenar un estadio con 80 mil personas y ponerles un solo de guitarra de 8 minutos y que la gente lo disfrute, que hoy es rarísimo, ¿ver eso?"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Ambition for Stardom
podcast.body: Matt Bellamy showed immense ambition early in Muse's career. Before breaking into North America, he expressed a desire to "try harder" when able to move freely in public. He also believed in playing every small gig, such as at the Monarch in London, "like it was Wembley Stadium" to prepare for future larger venues. "He looked at me and he said, no, this just means we have to try harder."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arpeggio Playing Style
podcast.body: He frequently uses arpeggios, playing the individual notes of a chord sequentially, which allows for dynamic transitions between arpeggiated lines and full chords. "First of all, he likes arpeggios. This is when you take the three notes of a chord and play them individually one after another in either ascending or descending order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chris Wolstenholme's College Move
podcast.body: Bass player Chris Wolstenholme, originally from Rotherham (a city of about 100,000), ended up in Teignmouth to attend community college, where he would later meet his bandmates. "Base player Chris Wolston-Holm is originally from Rotterham, city of about 100,000, but he ended up in 10mouth going to community college."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Classical Music Influences
podcast.body: Bellamy's style incorporates classical elements, with specific similarities noted between some Muse songs and compositions by Chopin and Rachmaninoff. "And if you want to get really nerdy, you can find similarities between some mu songs and Chopin and Rockman enough."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comparison to Eddie Van Halen
podcast.body: Matt Bellamy is considered the equivalent of Eddie Van Halen for the 2000s, recognized for his significant impact on guitar style, technique, and technology during that era. "What Eddie Van Halen was to the late 1970s and early 1980s, you could say that Matt is the equivalent to the 2000s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comparison to Queen
podcast.body: Mios's "epic rock" or "opera rock" sound, particularly on albums like "Absolution" and "de sé con lo," has drawn comparisons to Queen from some critics. "Se estaban yendo a ese especie de rock épico o peda rock que a veces recordaba demasiado a Queen."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Conceptual Album Approach
podcast.body: Many Mios albums, starting with "Absolution," were conceived as conceptual albums. However, critics often noted that their conceptual depth was not fully realized when compared to genuinely conceptual works by bands like Pink Floyd or King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard. "Aunque muchos discos de míos son conceptuales, distan mucho de considerar un álbum conceptual propiamente dicho, si lo comparas con álbumes conceptuales de verdad como los que puede hacer Pin Floyd o como álbumes conceptuales modernos como los que puede hacer King Gisa Randalizar Wizard."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Conspiracy Theories and Scientific Obsessions – Bilderbergs, 9/11 Truthers, Alien Reptile Royals
podcast.body: Bellamy at one time believed 9/11 was an inside job (he later recanted), is concerned about the Bilderberg Group and Trilateral Commission, and based "Unnatural Selection" on the Babylonian Brotherhood theory — the idea that the British Royal Family are descendants of giant alien lizards, as proposed by British writer David Icke. Right-wing conspiracy theorists began using Muse music in their internet videos, which greatly annoyed Bellamy — not because of the conspiracy usage but because he felt the right wing had "hijacked all the best conspiracies." A Muse fan-compiled reading list includes both fringe (Zecharia Sitchin's ancient alien theories) and legitimate scientific works (Brian Greene's *The Elegant Universe*, Orwell's *1984*). "He felt that the right wing had hijacked all the best conspiracies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continued Activity in 2010s
podcast.body: This established band continued its characteristic musical output throughout the 2010s, contrasting with the softer pop alt-rock trend. "Older groups, the food fighters, Lincoln Park, Black Keys, Chili Peppers, Green Day, Queens of the Stone Age, Royal Blood, Muse, Blink 182, Pearl Jam, they just kept doing what they did best."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Custom "Maddocasters" with Integrated Technology
podcast.body: His custom "Maddocasters," built by British luthier Hugh Manson, are known for incorporating various mysterious onboard technologies, making his unique sounds difficult to replicate. "his guitars are custom made by a British guy named Hugh Manson. He packs all kinds of weird technology on board into the guitar. He calls them Maddocasters"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dominic Howard's Family Relocation
podcast.body: Drummer Dominic Howard is originally from the Manchester area but moved with his family to Teignmouth when he was about eight years old. "And then there's drummer Dominic Howard. He's originally from the Manchester area, but moved with his family to 10mouth when he was about eight."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Band History
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, before becoming Muse, the core members played in high school bands. Matt Bellamy was the guitarist for Dominic Howard's band Carnage Mayhem, which evolved into Gothic Plague. They then formed Rocket Baby Dolls, embracing a "glam goth thing," before changing their name to Muse at a teacher's suggestion. "They were very much into a glam goth thing, but then at the behest of one of their teachers, they changed their name to Muse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Bands and Evolution
podcast.body: The three members of Muse initially played in separate bands at Teignmouth community college before forming a group called Gothic Plague, which later evolved into Rocket Baby Dolls. "The three guys played in separate bands at 10mouth community college before finally getting together in a group called Gothic Plague, which then evolved into Rocket Baby dolls."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Career Recording & Drug Use
podcast.body: Muse recorded *Origin of Symmetry* in Surrey around 2001 while in their early twenties and on tour, with sessions characterized by the band being "on mushrooms the entire time." David Botrell's main task was managing Matt Bellamy's overwhelming flow of creative ideas. "they were basically on mushrooms the entire time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Struggles and Day Jobs
podcast.body: For the next five years, the members of Muse worked as painters and decorators during the day, taking any jobs they could find. At night, they played in various pubs that would book them, enduring a difficult period to keep their musical aspirations alive. "For the next five years, they worked as painters and decorators by day, taking jobs wherever they could, and at night they played in whatever pubs would have them. It was awfully hard, but they kept at it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Vocal and Guitar Style Comparisons to Radiohead
podcast.body: Their debut album "Showbiz" had striking similarities to Radiohead's "OK Computer," from Matt Bellamy's singing style (which later changed significantly) to the "weeping, agonizing, tragic" guitar sound characteristic of "OK Computer." Guitar publications even compared the pedal structures used by both bands. "Los propios míos nunca se han declarado grandes fans de Radiohead de Tom York pero no podemos negar que había parecidos bastante importantes entre los dos discos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Emerging Big Band (2000s)
podcast.body: Muse is mentioned as one of the "soon-to-be-big bands" that emerged around 2000-2001, contributing to the broader landscape of revitalized rock music.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolutionary Challenges
podcast.body: While Mios has evolved over the years, they have struggled to truly evolve in a significant way, often falling back on their sonic clichés. "Es una banda que desde siempre ha sido un poco víctima de esos propios clichés sonoros, que si ha sabido evolucionar con los años, pero la que le ha costado mucho evolucionar de verdad."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Featured in Apple Commercials
podcast.body: Muse's music has been part of Apple's commercial campaigns, illustrating the company's practice of integrating well-known bands into its advertisements for products like the iPod and iPhone.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 2

podcast.title: First Gig as Muse
podcast.body: The band's performance at a battle of the bands contest in Torquay, Southern England, on November 26, 1994, where Matt Bellamy was 16, is suggested as possibly their first ever gig under the name Muse. "This could be the first ever gig that Muse played under their new name."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Great Musicianship
podcast.body: Mios members are widely recognized as great musicians and instrumentalists. "Ellos son unos grandísimos músicos, son unos grandísimos instrumentalistas, no se pueden negar."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: In-Ear Monitors Enable Energetic Performance
podcast.body: The use of in-ear monitors is cited as essential for Matt Bellamy, the frontman of Muse, enabling his highly dynamic and mobile stage presence, even in large venues like Wembley Stadium. The monitors provide him with a clear, personal mix regardless of his movement. "met Bellamy couldn't possibly run around as much as he does without in-ear monitors."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence from The Bends and OK Computer
podcast.body: Muse referenced both Radiohead's *The Bends* and *OK Computer* as influences, with a particular emphasis on *The Bends*. "News hizo referencia de Benz aunque también a lo que hay computer, pero sobre todo hizo mucha referencia de Benz."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: RADIOHEAD: THE BENDS desde otra perspectiva

podcast.title: Influence of Tool's Lateralus on Muse
podcast.body: Muse is acknowledged as a band heavily influenced by Tool's Lateralus, with references to the album appearing in their music and approach as early as 5 to 10 years after its release, and continuing to the present day. Matt Bellamy, a prominent member of Muse, is specifically mentioned for having drawn significant inspiration and used Lateralus as a key reference point in his artistic development. "Ha tenido como muchísima influencia de entro de mucha gente posterior, 5, 10 años después, incluso hay gente hoy en día. Pues como puede ser news que siempre han hecho muchísima referencia a la tralos de túl."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Local Battle of the Bands Victory
podcast.body: The band, then known as Rocket Baby Dolls, surprised themselves by winning a local battle of the bands contest. This victory made them consider that they might have a real chance at a musical career. "They were into this clam rock thing. Then after shocking themselves by winning a local battle of the band's contest, they began to think that maybe they did have a shot at doing something."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Maintaining Guitar Sound in a Dying Market
podcast.body: Mios released guitar-driven albums like "Showbiz" at a time when the guitar sound was considered "officially dead" in the UK after Radiohead's "OK Computer" in the mid-90s. They were one of the few bands keeping the guitar sound alive when it wasn't fashionable. "El sonido guitarrero estaba muriendo poco a poco a mitad de los 90 y al menos en el reino unido, no tanto en Estados Unidos pero sobre todo en el reino unido. Después del loque y computer es como un antesión después. Es la muerte oficial que ha sido el sonido de guitarra."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Matt Bellamy's Car Theft Ring – Stole a Ford Escort from the Wrong Guy
podcast.body: At 18, having moved from Teignmouth to Exeter to live above a porn store with a painter/drug dealer friend, Bellamy got involved in a small-time car theft ring, stealing cheap vehicles for modest profit. The scheme fell apart when he stole a Ford Escort belonging to someone dangerous, who showed up demanding £500 or he would harm Bellamy and his family. Lacking the money, Bellamy handed over the band's touring van. "So much for a career in Grand Theft Auto."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Matt Bellamy's Creative Flow
podcast.body: Matt Bellamy is described as an "inspiring character" with a constant flow of ideas. During overdubs, he would frequently interrupt to pursue new keyboard ideas, requiring the producer to record snippets and then guide him back to the original task. "He'd be in the middle of a guitar overdub halfway through the song. Oh, wait, I've got this keyboard thing. Hang on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Matt Bellamy's Family Relocation
podcast.body: Singer Matt Bellamy's family moved to Teignmouth in the mid-1980s when he was around eight years old. "Charles and singer Matt Bellamy's family moved here in the mid-1980s when he was around eight years old."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mixed Critical Reception
podcast.body: Mios's albums have consistently received mixed reviews, similar to Queen. There are two main critical camps: one that considers them a great rock band at a time when rock was not popular, and another that views them as monotonous, repetitive, and not contributing much new to the music market. "Es curioso porque con esta banda siempre nos ha pasado un poco, pues, como con Quink, que las críticas de sus iscos siempre han sido bastante mixtas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Multi-Talented Musician
podcast.body: Beyond his technical guitar proficiency, Matt Bellamy possesses a three-octave vocal range, is an accomplished piano player, is adept in a recording studio, and is constantly seeking new sounds. "Not only is he technically proficient, okay, very proficient, he also has a three octave vocal range. He's an excellent piano player. He knows his way around a recording studio and he never, ever stops looking for new sounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Name Change and Career Commitment
podcast.body: On the advice of one of their teachers, the band changed their name to Muse. They then decided to forgo university, quit their day jobs, and move away from Teignmouth to pursue music full-time. "On the advice of one of their teachers, they changed their name to Muse, decided to skip university, quit their jobs, and moved away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Name Origin – Occult Witchcraft Sessions with Three Girls
podcast.body: The name "Muse" may have come from a teacher introducing Bellamy to the word, but the preferred explanation involves three girls from school who practiced witchcraft in abandoned houses, casting spells. Matt — who was attracted to one of them — tagged along and played guitar during the sessions. "He thought one of them was kind of hot, so he went with her and the other two friends to abandoned houses where they cast spells."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: North American Breakthrough Delay
podcast.body: Despite performing in arenas across Europe, Muse continued to play clubs in North America until the release of their fourth album, indicating a slower path to prominence on that continent. "They might have been playing arenas in Europe, but when it came to their fourth album, they were still playing clubs on this side of the Atlantic."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Paranoid and Surreal Lyrics
podcast.body: Starting from "Black Holes and Rebellations," Matt Bellamy's lyrics began to feature paranoid and surreal themes, discussing conspiracies and aliens. On "de sé con lo," these "paranoid lyrics" were described as "bordering on the ridiculous." "Empieza a esa especie de letras un poco paranoicas y surrealistas que tiene más velami hablando de conspiraciones y de marcianos y de bueno."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Recipient of Marketing Investment
podcast.body: Muse is an example of an established performer who still receives marketing investment from record labels, in contrast to the limited support for emerging rock acts. "Any money that is available goes to performers who already have a track record like, uh, muse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Trying to be a Superstar in the 21st Century

podcast.title: Recording at Abbey Road Studios
podcast.body: Muse is among the list of legendary artists and bands who have made albums at the historic Abbey Road Studios in London. "I mean, Beatles, Pink Floyd, Oasis, Blur, Muse, Kate Bush, DePeshmo, Iron Maiden, Queen, You Tube Michael Jackson, Glenn Miller. They all made albums there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Recording at Air Lyndhurst Hall
podcast.body: Muse was a client at Air Lyndhurst Hall, George Martin's studio in North London, known for its expansive hexagonal Studio One that can accommodate orchestras and choirs. "Clients have included you too, Adele, Kate Bush, Liam Gallagher, Coldplay Muse, and Mumford and Sons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Release Coincided with Shifting Trends (Origin of Symetry)
podcast.body: "Origin of Symetry" was released months after Radiohead's "Kid A" sparked a UK craze for experimental electronic progressive rock, and simultaneously with The Strokes' debut, which launched a "garage rock revival." This left Mios somewhat isolated. "Porque justo unos meses antes del lanzamiento Origin of Symetry salía el quide y de Radiohead con lo cual se desatabó en una especie de furor dentro del reino unido por ese rock experimental el electrónico progresivo a raro uno se desatabó en auténtica fiebre después del quide y dentro del reino unido."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Repetitive Sonic Clichés
podcast.body: Mios has often been criticized for getting "stuck in their own clichés," particularly after "Absolution." This includes reiterating an epic sound, heavy piano use, and Matt Bellamy's increasingly forceful vocals, leading to a perception of being un-evolved. "Un poco míos se empezaría a quedar un poco atascado en sus propios cliches."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Self-Production on de resistance
podcast.body: A significant career change for Mios was their decision to self-produce "de resistance," which is considered by many to be a major mistake. This move, without external producers to provide a fresh perspective, led to their sound becoming self-referential and increasingly "more Mios," reinforcing their own stylistic patterns. "En este album también tenemos uno de los más importantes cambios a la carrera de míos que para mucha gente es posiblemente el mayor error de la carrera de míos, que es que en este album han pasado a producirse a sí mismos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Sheep Farming
podcast.body: Matt Bellamy is keenly interested in sheep farming, with a flock of nearly 200 sheep, effectively making him a shepherd. "It's not terribly well known, but Matt Bellamy of Muse is really into sheep farming. He has nearly 200 sheep."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Teignmouth, Devon Origins - Population 14,748
podcast.body: Muse was formed in Teignmouth, Devon, England, a town with a population of 14,748 located in the southwest of England. The band's members, though not all born there, moved to the town at young ages and met there. "Our next stop is Tainmouth, population 14,748. You'll find this place in the southwest of England."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Guardian's Harsh Review of Origin of Symetry
podcast.body: The album "Origin of Symetry" received a very low rating of "one" from The Guardian newspaper, which considered its guitar sound outdated and boring. "De hecho jamás lo olvidaré y lo tengo que volver a decir en su día de Guardian le dio un uno, un puto, uno que coño me cuentas un uno al origen a Jimmy Hendrix de míos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: Twilight Saga Influence
podcast.body: Muse's music was a significant influence on Stephenie Meyer, the author of *The Twilight Saga* novels, who did a lot of her writing while listening to their music. Consequently, Muse made the cut for the movie soundtracks, appearing on the various *Twilight* discs. "Stephanie Myers, the author of The Novels in which the movies were based, is a big fan of muse. She did a lot of writing to their music, so it's no surprise that they made the cut for the movie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: UK Alt Rock Success (2010s)
podcast.body: Muse was identified as one of the "monsters" in the UK alt-rock scene that did well during the 2010s. "Meanwhile, the Monsters did well, and that would include Coldplay and Muse and Gorillas."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Use of Backing Tracks in Live Shows
podcast.body: Muse, a three-member band, employs backing tracks in their live performances to augment their sound and replicate the intricate layers of their studio recordings. While the core three members play their parts live, additional pre-recorded audio is integrated to enrich the overall sound, demonstrating a common and accepted practice for enhancing live production quality in modern music. "For example, there are three guys in muse and to replicate their sounds they need additional help."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 5: (60-51)

podcast.title: Victim of Self-Generated Expectations
podcast.body: A recurring issue throughout Mios's career, particularly for Matt Bellamy, is the problem of being a victim of his own generated expectations. He would often state in interviews, months before an album's release, that it would be groundbreaking, electronic, or radically different, only for the actual release to be perceived as an update of existing sounds. This pattern has led to public disappointment and a loss of credibility. "Uno de los problemas que siempre ha tenido más velami es que es víctima de las propias expectativas que el mismo genera, cuando tú te pasas seis meses antes del lanzamiento del disco, diciendo en las entrevistas que vas a hacer un álbum rompedor, el electrónico, radicalmente distinto a lo que había hecho en ese momento y luego saca eso, la gente se siente excepcionada."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La discografía de MUSE disco a disco, con lo bueno y con lo malo

podcast.title: World Record Guitar Smasher
podcast.body: Matt Bellamy of Muse holds the Guinness Book of World Records title for destroying the most guitars. During the band's 2004 tour, which supported their "Absolution" album, he totaled 140 guitars. "The all-time champion guitar smasher is... Oh, it's not Pete Townsend of the Hoot. It's Matt Bellamy of Muse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Worst Offenders in Loudness Wars
podcast.body: Muse is specifically named as one of the "worst offenders" among bands whose recent albums suffer from excessive compression, leading to an unrelenting loudness that causes listener fatigue. "The worst offenders that I found are the Arctic monkeys, the chili peppers, the killers, mues, queens of the Stone Age, and of course Metallica."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

concerts.title: Battle of the Bands (Nov 26, 1994) - Torquay, Southern England
concerts.body: On this date, Muse played a battle of the bands contest in Torquay. This gig, where Matt Bellamy was 16 years old, might have been their first performance under the name Muse, following their previous incarnation as Rocket Baby Dolls. "On November 26th of 1994, they played a battle of the band's contest. This could be the first ever gig that Muse played under their new name."
